messages.subject: Comparing frequency ranges across corpora
messages.body_plain:
Hello group,

A colleague and I have a question regarding comparing frequency ranges across corpora. It's not a technical question, but I hope it's not too off topic for the group.

In our English data we have frequency counts dervived from the Contemporary Corpus of American English (COCA) and SUBTLEXus (tv/film subtitle) corpora and we have noted that the frequency ranges differ widely: 1-550 in COCA, 1-1500 in SUBTLEXus (per million).  Our goal is to identify words that are matched, for example as high frequency, in both corpora and then identify words that are mismatched: one being high frequency and the other either mid or low frequency, and so on through mid and low frequency ranges.

One way to compare these samples is to identify and categorize words as High, Mid and Low frequency relative to each sample independently and then match the categorized words across the samples. However, since our goal in selecting these frequency ranges is to create materials for a psycholinguistic experiment to gauge speakers' behavioral reaction to contrasting frequency counts, ( via lexical decision and subjective word familiarity tasks) it seems strange that the range, of say Low in COCA, may be from 1 to ~200 yet in SUBTLEXus Low is something like 1 to ~500, almost eclipsing the entire frequency range for COCA. Yet we have also noted that there is a relationship between frequency range and lexical diversity -- the bigger the range, the less lexically diverse the sample.
We were wondering how one might approach reconciling these lexical differences in our samples, and whether there is a need, and if so, a principled method for deriving a frequency score that compensates for lexical diversity in a sample providing a potentially more reliable cross-sample frequency score.

We'd love to hear some thoughts on this.

Thanks,

messages.subject: Re: [CorpLing with R] Comparing frequency ranges across corpora
messages.subject_clean: [CorpLing with R] Comparing frequency ranges across corpora
messages.body_plain:
Hello Jerid,
We've used the log likelihood ratio (LLR) statistic over two corpora to see which words appear more frequently than expected in an individual corpora. We have a couple of papers under review describing our work (feel free to contact me for a pre-publication copy if interested), or it is described in Chapter 4 of my PhD thesis [1]. You could of course categorise the words according to the quantitative LLR scores if desired.

Another option is to use a chi-squared test, but for linguistic frequency data it's not so appropriate due to how it copes with smaller frequencies.

Some references below [2][3][4].

Hope this is helpful,
Anna

Refs:
[1] http://kcl.academia.edu/AnnaJordanous/Papers/859375/Evaluating_Computational_Creativity_A_Standardised_Procedure_for_Evaluating_Creative_Systems_and_its_Application
[2] Dunning, T. 1993. Accurate methods for the statistics of surprise and coincidence. Computational Linguistics 19(1):61–74.
[3] Rayson, P., and Garside, R. 2000. Comparing corpora using frequency profiling. In Proceedings of ACL Workshop on Comparing Corpora.
[4] Kilgarriff, A. 2001. Comparing corpora. International Journal of Corpus Linguistics 6(1):97–133.

messages.subject: question about the "rhyme sequence" example on page 89 of the book
messages.subject_clean: question about the "rhyme sequence" example on page 89 of the book
messages.body_plain:
Hello group,

On the P89 of the book there's an example code about adding an "<r>" to every potential rhyme sequence in a sentence. Here's the code:

text <- c("This is a first example sentence.", "And this is a second example sentence.")
gsub("(\\w+?)(\\W+\\w*?)\\1(\\W)", "\\1<r>\\2\\1<r>\\3", text, perl=T)

I can understand this and the code works perfectly, but what about the situation that the rhyme sequence contains more than two words, for example:
text[3] <- "This is a nice example sentence."

Now the result would be "This<r> is<r> a nice<r> example<r> sentence.". Obviously the "example" is consumed in replacing the "nice example" pair, as a result the "example sentence" pair is omitted. However "This<r> is<r> a nice<r> example<r> sentence<r>." is actually my intended result. Any suggestions on the solution?

Thanks!

text.new <http://text.new> <- gsub("(\\w+?)\\b(.+\\w*)\\1\\b", "\\1<r>\\2\\1<r>", text, perl=TRUE)
for (i in 1:10) {
   # both orders of already tagged/untagged matches
   text.new <http://text.new> <- gsub("((\\w+?)<r>)(.+?)(\\2)(?!<r>)\\b",
"\\1\\3\\4<r>", text.new <http://text.new>, perl=TRUE)
   text.new <http://text.new> <- gsub("(\\w+?)(?!<r>)\\b(.*?)(\\1<r>)", "\\1<r>\\2\\3",
text.new <http://text.new>, perl=TRUE)
}

messages.subject: Re: Exercise Box 3.7(2)(b) in QCLWR
messages.body_plain: On Mar 4, 4:04 pm, "Stefan Th. Gries" wrote: > I think the error is because Gabor has revised gsubfn a few times, the > code in the answer key did work at publication time. Plus, I think > there may be a mistake on the help page of gsubfn here because Gabor's > own most similar example doesn't seem to work either. His help page > says: > > library(gsubfn) > # makes all letters except first in word lower case > gsubfn("\\B.", tolower, "I LIKE A BANANA SPLIT", perl = TRUE) The bug is that when gsubfn uses the tcl engine gsubfn ignores perl = TRUE whereas what it should be doing is to switch to the R engine so that it can use perl regular expressions. Since \B means backslash (rather than non-boundary) in tcl regular expressions we get the problem. A workaround is to force the R engine by using engine = "R": gsubfn("\\B.", tolower, "I LIKE A BANANA SPLIT", perl = TRUE, engine = "R") or options(gsubfn.engine = "R") gsubfn("\\B.", tolower, "I LIKE A BANANA SPLIT", perl = TRUE) although setting the option will impact performance of other statements that would have otherwise used tcl since tcl is faster. Thus if you set the option you might want to change it back afterwards: options(gsubfn.engine = NULL) This attempt: > gsubfn("([a-zA-Z]+)(?=)", toupper("\\1"),text, perl=T) ignores perl = T; however, perl = T is not really needed as the regular expression works in the tcl engine too so the bug described above does not really prevent it from working. Rather, the problem is that toupper("\\1") is not valid. Evidently what was desired was a function that operates only on the first (...) part. To do that try: gsubfn("([a-zA-Z]+)(?=)", ~ toupper(..1), text) or the solution using the backref argument shown in the prior post.

On Sat, Mar 24, 2012 at 11:42 PM, Bob Green <bgr...@dyson.brisnet.org.au> wrote:

> I was hoping for some advice regarding creating a data file(s) from R Digests. I save these files into my mail program (Eudora) but they are now in several folders because of the space they take up. To speed up my mail program and to facilitate searches, I was planning on using R to do searches. I know there are search engines on the Cran site but often it can be difficult locating specific topics.

With other lists, which are much more prolific than this or R-users, I have kept archives in mbox format. When I need to search through the messages (in either text or RFC-x821/x822 headers) the grep utility comes in handy to locate the message(s) of interest. Depending upon my need the -A or -B options may be necessary to give the surrounding context. Or depending on the version of grep installed the --after-context and --before-context options respectively.

However, if I needed extended searches over email texts I would use one of the search systems available; either mg from the Witten/Moffat/Bell book "Managing Gigabytes" or Lucene from Apache. Both are freely available as source code. Lucene is available as pre-built binaries ready for the Java Virtual Machine. Lucene also has a richer search language. Whereas in the past I would have used mg today I'd be going for Lucene.

If my intent in putting messages archives into R so as to analyse the texts in some way, maybe using the tm module, I would seriously thinking about adding in a Lucene support module to R --- someone may already have done that anyway.

> Any suggestions regarding the above or comments on issues, that I should consider, are appreciated,

You should clarify what it is that you want to search for and choose an appropriate tool: grep, mg or Lucene, or something else. Don't be beguiled by the fact that as your archives contain R mailing list messages you must then use R to process them. Use R only for what it is good for; use support tools for what they are good for; if necessary combine them together and assist us all by so doing.

Regards, Trevor.
